tip: Money uses Sino numbers: 오십만 원 (osimman won) = 500,000 won.
Bills 'come out' in Korean: 카드값이 이번 달에 많이 나왔어요 (kadeugapsi ibeon dare mani nawasseoyo) = the card bill came out high this month. 나오다 (naoda = come out) is how charges show up.
긁다 (geukda) literally means 'scratch' – Korean pictures card spending as scratching the card: 카드를 긁었어요 (kadeureul geulgeosseoyo) = I swiped my card.
-보다 = than: 현금보다 (hyeongeumboda) = than cash.
Fees stick on in Korean: 수수료가 붙었어요 (susuryoga buteosseoyo) uses 붙다 (butda) 'stick' – the fee attached itself to the transfer.
-아/어서 = and then: 전화해서 (jeonhwahaeseo) = called, and then...
정해져 있어요 (jeonghaejeo isseoyo) uses -아/어 있어요 (-a/eo isseoyo) for a state that was set and stays set – the limit isn't being set now, it already sits there fixed.
-아/어야 해요 (-a/eoya haeyo) means 'have to': 내야 해요 (naeya haeyo) = must pay. Literally 'only if you pay does it work' – obligation built from a condition.
-한테 usually means 'to', but with 빌렸어요 (billyeosseoyo = borrowed) it flips to 'from': 친구한테 (chinguhante) = from a friend. The verb decides the direction.
-(으)ㄹ게요 = I promise to: 갚을게요 (gapeulgeyo) = I'll pay it back.
-(으)면 = if: 받으면 (badeumyeon) = if you take/receive it.
A whole clause can sit before a noun: 이자가 낮은 은행 (ijaga najeun eunhaeng) = 'interest-is-low bank' – Korean front-loads the description English puts after.
-보다 (-boda) marks the compared thing and 더 (deo) spells out 'more': 수입보다 지출이 더 많아요 (suip-boda jichuri deo manayo) = spending exceeds income. 더 is optional but adds punch.
Costs go in, in Korean: 들다 (deulda) 'enter' is the cost verb – 생활비가 많이 들어요 (saenghwalbiga mani deureoyo) = living costs 'go in' a lot, i.e. they're high.
-(으)면 안 돼요 = must not: 넘으면 안 돼요 (neomeumyeon an dwaeyo).
-(으)려고 해요 = intend to: 사려고 해요 (saryeogo haeyo) = plan to buy.
Korean costs 'enter': 교육비가 정말 많이 들어요 (gyoyukbiga jeongmal mani deureoyo) = education really costs a lot, literally 'education money enters'. 들다 (deulda), no separate verb 'to cost'.
-(이)랑 = with: 남편이랑 (nampyeon-irang) = with my husband.
What you become takes 이/가 (i/ga), not an object marker: 습관이 됐어요 (seupgwani dwaesseoyo) = became a habit. With 되다 (doeda), the result acts like a subject.
갚는 거예요 (gamneun geoyeyo) wraps the verb in -는 거 (-neun geo) = 'the act of paying off' – how Korean states a goal: my goal IS the paying-off, a noun-like thing.
현명하게 (hyeonmyeonghage) = wisely; -게 makes an adverb.
입학하다 (iphakada = to enroll) takes 에: 대학교에 입학해요 (daehakgyoe iphakaeyo).
시 (si = o'clock) takes native numbers: 아홉 시 (ahop si = nine o'clock).
께서 (kkeseo) marks an honored subject and pairs with -세요: 교수님께서 하세요 (gyosunimkkeseo haseyo).
층 (cheung = floor) uses Sino numbers: 삼 층 (sam cheung = 3rd floor).
전공하다 (jeongonghada = to major) takes 을/를: 경영학을 전공해요 (gyeongyeonghageul jeongonghaeyo).
이에요/예요 = 'is': after a consonant 공학이에요 (gonghagieyo); after a vowel 친구예요 (chinguyeyo).
과목 (gwamok = course) counts with native numbers: 여섯 과목 (yeoseot gwamok = six courses).
-(이)나 (-ina) means 'as many as': 세 개나 (se gaena = as many as three).
하고 (hago = with) joins people: 룸메이트하고 (rummeiteuhago = with a roommate).
